paper_title: Reading, Not Adapting: Unlocking Frozen Visual Knowledge for AI-Generated Image Detection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates a shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers a direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers-inspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within a fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as a promising alternative to backbone adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/yunncheng/ReMoT.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, Mixture-of-Transformersinspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as promising alternative to backbone adaptation. 1. Introduction The rapid evolution of image generation poses fundamental challenge to AI-generated image detection: generalizing beyond the generators encountered during training. Detectors must recognize unseen synthesis methods [37] while remaining robust to variations in image content, source distributions, and post-processing [17]. Yet learned forensic *Corresponding author Figure 1. Generalization across eight benchmarks. Axes report balanced accuracy; parentheses give eight-group averages. cues [30, 35, 38] may capture generator-specific artifacts or dataset biases rather than transferable evidence of synthesis [5, 12, 25, 47]. UnivFD [23] provided early evidence of the potential of pretrained visual knowledge, demonstrating transferable detection using frozen CLIP [26] representations and simple classifiers. Motivated by this potential, considerable research has focused on adapting pretrained backbones to improve cross-generator generalization. Methods such as FatFormer [21] and Effort [40] modify pretrained feature processing for detection while seeking to preserve transferable visual knowledge. Recent findings, however, challenge whether such adaptation is always necessary. Simplicity Prevails [45] demonstrates that modern vision foundation models (VFMs), particularly DINOv3 [27], already encode highly transferable 1 Figure 2. From backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Representative designs: (A) task-trained backbone adaptation; (B) heterogeneous encoding with late fusion; (C) final-layer RGB linear probing; (D) frozen dual-view joint processing with staged interaction and progressive query readout. detection knowledge accessible through simple linear probing. Moreover, additional adaptation, including LoRA [14], can substantially degrade generalization in its evaluated settings. These findings motivate shift in emphasis from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Yet how to effectively exploit this knowledge remains underexplored. Conventional frozen linear probing typically relies on single final-layer RGB representation, leaving complementary evidence across views and Transformer depth largely unexploited. Meanwhile, multi-cue detectors incorporate semantic, spatial, and frequency-related evidence, but representative approaches often involve adaptation, heterogeneous encoding, and late fusion [6, 39]. These designs entail distinct tradeoffs: adaptation may favor training-specific patterns; heterogeneous encoders produce representations with different inductive biases and abstraction levels, complicating their integration; and late fusion prevents intermediate interaction between independently encoded views. This leaves fundamental question: how can frozen encoders with the same architecture jointly exploit complementary forensic evidence beyond final-layer RGB probing? Our central insight is that organizing complementary evidence and learning how to read it can better exploit pretrained detection knowledge without learning task-specific visual transformations. Complementary views can interact within common pretrained architecture, while their evidence can be accessed throughout feature extraction. Crossview interaction and readout determine how this knowledge is accessed. Effective readout therefore involves both crossview organization and access across Transformer depth. We realize this perspective in ReMoT (Readout with Mixtureof-Transformers), framework for progressive cross-view readout in AI-generated image detection. MoT [20] combines modality-specific Transformer parameters with joint attention across modalities. ReMoT adopts this principle for spatially aligned RGB and discrete wavelet transform (DWT) views. Both streams use the same frozen DINOv3 architecture and pretrained weights, providing common foundation for MoT-inspired joint attention. staged jointattention mechanism initially preserves view-specific processing and subsequently enables controlled cross-view interaction through local patch correspondence and global register-mediated communication. Meanwhile, learnable fusion queries progressively read both views across Transformer depth using frozen attention projections, without writing back to view tokens. Together, these mechanisms organize cross-view evidence for progressive readout while preserving pretrained backbone weights. Trained solely on GenImage Stable Diffusion v1.4 (SD v1.4), ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups (Figure 1) with only 3,074 trainable parameters in its equivalent implementation, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. An independently trained variant without direct cross-view interaction reaches 87.0%, highlighting the value of evidence exchange alongside progressive query readout. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We advance readout-centered perspective for generalizable detection, shifting the design focus from adapting pretrained representations to organizing and accessing their existing detection knowledge. 2. We propose ReMoT, combining frozen RGB/DWT 2 Figure 3. ReMoT framework. Frozen RGB/DWT streams interact from block s; fusion queries progressively read both without writeback. Insets show spatial alignment, joint attention, and Stage II connectivity (Figure 4). Only fusion-query embeddings and the classification head are trainable. DWT tiles are individually rescaled for display. streams, staged MoT-inspired joint attention with local patch and global register exchange, and learnable fusion queries for progressive readout across depth without writing back to either visual stream. 3. ReMoT achieves leading 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups, outperforming prior adaptation-based detectors and showing the potential of knowledge readout for generalizable detection. whether further adaptation is necessary. Simplicity Prevails [45] finds that modern VFMs, including DINOv3 [27], already support strong generalization through linear probing, while additional adaptation can degrade performance in its evaluated settings. These findings motivate readout beyond final-layer probing: ReMoT explores how existing visual knowledge can be accessed across views and depth while backbone weights remain frozen. 2. Related work 2.1. From adaptation to readout Generator-specific artifacts and dataset biases limit crossgenerator detection [5, 12]. UnivFD [23] demonstrated the value of pretrained knowledge through simple classifiers on frozen CLIP [26] features. Self-supervised foundations offer another source of transferable visual features [24]. Subsequent adaptation methods seek stronger detection representations while preserving transferability: FatFormer [21] introduces forgery-aware transformations, and Effort [40] learns in an orthogonal subspace while freezing principal pretrained components. Prompt-based methods likewise adapt pretrained representations for detection [32, 36]. OmniAID [13] decouples content-dependent semantic flaws from universal artifacts through routable semantic experts and an always-active artifact expert. Complementary reconstruction-based training improves crossgenerator generalization [4, 29]; DDA [5] aligns real and synthetic images in pixel and frequency domains to suppress spurious correlations. Recent evidence questions 2.2. Cross-view evidence integration Beyond final-layer RGB probing, complementary evidence can be sought across image views and Transformer depth. Local artifact modeling [19, 31, 34, 44], reconstruction [7], and quantization cues [42] complement RGB appearance. Spectral analyses caution against universal fingerprints [3, 10], motivating robust spectral representations [15, 16, 18]. Layer Consistency Matters [41] identifies evidence in latent transitions across layers. Multi-cue detectors and multimodal reasoning [46] explore evidence integration: AIDE [39] integrates semantic features with forensic features from texture-selected patches, while CO-SPY [6] enhances and adaptively fuses semantic and pixel-level features. However, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature alignment, and late fusion limits exchange during feature extraction. Developed for multimodal pretraining, MoT [20] combines trainable modality-specific Transformer parameters with joint self-attention. ReMoT borrows this joint-processing principle to exchange and progressively read spatially aligned RGB and wavelet evidence [22] using frozen pretrained backbones. 3 3. Only the fusion-query embeddings and shared classifier are optimized; all pretrained backbone parameters and input projections remain frozen. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental setup Implementation details. We train ReMoT on single NVIDIA H200 GPU using only the GenImage SD v1.4 training partition for ten epochs, including one warmup epoch. The model uses frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16, 336336 inputs, one-level db2 DWT, two fusion queries, stage boundary of = 9, and cross-view patch radius = 5. The readout is optimized with class-weighted cross-entropy, batch size 96, NAdam, learning rate 7.5 105, and weight decay 0.05. We apply Gaussian blur, JPEG compression, resizing, and noise augmentations. The exact equivalent implementation uses 3,074 trainable parameters (Appendix C); preprocessing is detailed in Appendix A. All ReMoT evaluations use the same trained model, without dataset-specific fine-tuning or threshold adjustments. Evaluation benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate across eight benchmark groups: GenImage (GI) [47], AIGCDetectBench (AIGCB) [43], EvalGEN [5], Synthbuster (SynB) [1], Mirage-Test (Mir) [13], Chameleon (Cham) [39], SynthWildX (SynX) [8], and WildRF [2]. Following DDA [5], we reduce format bias by JPEGcompressing synthetic images in GenImage and AIGCDetectBench at quality 96 (GI-QF96 and AIGCB-QF96). We report balanced accuracy to account for class imbalance (accuracy for single-class subsets), averaging subsets within groups and weighting all eight groups equally. Comparative methods. We compare ReMoT with NPR [31], UnivFD [23], FatFormer [21], SAFE [19], C2PCLIP [32], AIDE [39], DRCT [4], AlignedForensics [29], Effort [40], DDA [5], and OmniAID [13]. 5 Table 2. Main results Broad cross-benchmark transfer. ReMoT ranks first on five groups and second on three, averaging 91.2%  (Table 1)  . Mirage-Test exposes severe transfer failures among baselines, with even the strongest reaching only 55.7%, versus ReMoTs 84.1%. The lead also holds across the other seven groups: ReMoT averages approximately 92.2%, ahead of DDAs 90.1%. Transfer also spans unseen generators in GIQF96/AIGCB-QF96 (Tables 2 and 3) and nonphotographic Anime images in Mirage-Test (84.83%). Together, these results show that ReMoTs overall advantage is sustained across diverse benchmarks rather than driven by an isolated gain on single dataset. Consistency and class balance. ReMoT combines high accuracy with the lowest eight-group standard deviation (3.8 points), indicating consistent transfer. Mirage-Test further reveals class-prediction bias  (Table 4)  : SAFE and AlignedForensics classify almost all photographic inputs as real, whereas C2P-CLIP strongly favors fake predictions. ReMoT has the smallest realfake accuracy gap in all four photographic categories, with both class accuracies above 78%. This balanced operating point combines substantially higher fake-image recall than DDA with real-image accuracy above 80% in every photographic category. On Synthbuster, higher mean also accompanies lower subset variability (Appendix Table 7). These patterns support transfer beyond narrow training-generator cues. In-the-wild generalization. Deployment requires generalization to diverse, uncontrolled image sources. Trained solely on SD v1.4, ReMoT is the only compared detector reaching at least 90% on all three in-the-wild benchmarks  (Table 1)  . Knowledge readout thus enables transfer from single training generator to real-world images, supporting deployment without source-specific adaptation. 4.3. Ablation studies The ablations support learning to read frozen features and combining complementary views through selective interaction  (Table 6)  . This comparison supports learning to read pretrained features rather than learning taskspecific feature transformations. For the input views, RGBonly and DWT-only query readouts achieve 86.6% and 68.0%: RGB provides the stronger individual evidence, while combining both yields the best average. Retaining fusion-query readout while disabling cross-view attention (s = 24) yields 87.0%, 4.2 points below ReMoT. ReMoT improves seven of eight groups, most notably SynthWildX (+7.1 points) and WildRF (+11.3); EvalGEN scores are 96.3% and 98.0%, respectively. The mask variants then examine how views should communicate: local patch attention alone and global register attention alone reach 89.6% and 89.1%, versus 91.2% with both. Both ablations preserve within-view attention and query readout, supporting complementary local correspondence and global communication. Making patch attention global instead yields 90.5%, with lower scores on all eight groups despite retaining global register communication. These results favor spatially selective patch exchange alongside global register communication. Among mask variants, local-only leads on GI-QF96 and EvalGEN, and register-only on WildRF; combining both pathways provides the strongest overall transfer. Additional parameter studies appear in Appendix D. 4.4. Robustness to image post-processing ReMoT combines high post-processing accuracy with strong performance retention (Figure 5). On Chameleon, ReMoT retains 86.3% accuracy under JPEG quality 60 and 86.4% at blur radius 2.0, preserving 95.7% and 95.8% of its unmodified accuracy. DDA retains 89.8% and 89.4%, respectively, so ReMoTs relative accuracy loss is less than half as large. At these strongest tested severities, its margin over DDA widens from 7.8 points on unmodified images to 12.3 and 12.8 points. The gain thus reflects both stronger 7 Table 6. On original GenImage, ReMoT obtains 83.0% under JPEG quality 60 and 81.2% at blur radius 2.0; DDA reaches 89.0% and 89.2%. On Mirage-Test, ReMoT leads all compared methods under all eight degradation settings by at least 19.1 points. JPEG quality 60 yields 76.5%, retaining 90.9% of its unmodified accuracy, while blur radius 2.0 yields 85.3%, exceeding its 84.1% baseline. 5. Conclusion We proposed ReMoT to address transfer risks from backbone adaptation and the limited scope of existing readout approaches. It couples staged cross-view interaction with progressive evidence collection across Transformer 8 depth, while keeping pretrained backbone weights frozen. Trained on single generator, ReMoT achieves broad crossbenchmark generalization, balanced predictions, and strong robustness to image post-processing. These findings motivate research focus on readout design: organizing complementary evidence and learning how to access pretrained knowledge provide an effective basis for generalization across unfamiliar generators and diverse image sources.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: A. Additional implementation and reproducibility details Baseline sources. We use published baseline scores where available and otherwise evaluate the authors released checkpoints. We obtain most published scores from DDA [5] and published Mirage-Test scores from OmniAID [13]. Where DDAs reported benchmark averages differ from the arithmetic means of its listed subset scores, we retain the subset scores and recompute the corresponding averages. GI-QF96 and AIGCB-QF96 apply JPEG quality 96 to synthetic images in GenImage and AIGCDetectBench, respectively. Evaluation metrics. For subsets containing both classes, balanced accuracy is the mean of real-image and fake-image classification accuracy. For fake-only subsets, including EvalGEN and the Anime subset of Mirage-Test, we report fake-image classification accuracy, since real-image accuracy cannot be computed without real samples. All subsets use the same fixed decision threshold of 0.5. Subset scores are averaged within each benchmark group, and the overall average assigns equal weight to all eight group means. Wavelet embedding and augmentation. The frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 has 24 blocks of hidden width 1024 and four register tokens per view. DWT is computed on the augmented RGB image in [0, 1], before RGB normalization. For 336 336 input, zero-padded db2 subbands are cropped to 168 168 by retaining their first 168 rows and columns. The frozen 12-channel DWT patch stem is obtained by subsampling the pretrained RGB 16 16 kernel into an 8 8 kernel, repeating its input channel weights over four wavelet subbands, and scaling both the weights and bias by 1/4. The two aligned patch grids use matching 2D RoPE coordinates. Gaussian blur uses σ [0, 3]; JPEG compression, resizing, and noise have application probabilities of 0.15, 0.5, and 0.1, respectively, with randomized augmentation order. During evaluation, all preprocessing operations are deterministic. Query initialization and ablation provenance. The two logical fusion queries are initialized from the same pretrained class embedding; the equivalent implementation stores one query with fixed fusion-key bias. The DINOv3 linear probe trains classification head on frozen RGB ViT-L/16 class-token features using the GenImage SD v1.4 training partition. The single-view query readouts use either RGB or DWT inputs. The no-interaction model retains both views and the same fusion-query pathway, with = 24 disabling direct cross-view token attention in all blocks. B. Additional generator-level results Tables 7 and 8 provide the per-generator results on Synthbuster and EvalGEN, respectively, showing how performance varies across generators within each benchmark. C. Exact reparameterizations and efficiency Design and equivalent implementation. ReMoTs MoTinspired formulation assigns separate Transformer parameter slots to the RGB and DWT streams and uses fusion queries for progressive readout. Under our training setup, we find that ReMoT admits more compact, exactly equivalent implementation. It shares the slot weights and replaces the queries with one query and fixed attention bias, preserving both visual streams, their staged interaction, and the models predictions. Weight sharing relies on identical slot parameters, which we maintain by freezing both slots at the same pretrained initialization. Query reduction relies on identical initial query states and symmetric computation at every layer. Modality-specific updates that make the slot weights differ or query-specific changes that break symmetry invalidate the respective equivalence. Frozen Transformer-slot sharing. The MoT-inspired formulation assigns RGB and DWT tokens to view-specific In ReMoT, however, both Transformer parameter slots. slots are initialized from the same pretrained DINOv3 checkpoint and remain frozen. Denote all parameters of block ℓ in view by Θm,ℓ, including normalization, QKV and output projections, and the feed-forward network. Then Θr,ℓ = Θd,ℓ = Θℓ for every block. Replacing both view-specific parameter slots with the shared parameters Θℓ therefore preserves the projections of every token: (Qℓ, Kℓ, Vℓ)MoT = (Qℓ, Kℓ, Vℓ)shared. Importantly, this shares parameters, not view tokens: the two input stems, all view-token computations, and all stagedependent cross-view connections remain intact. Equality of the two slot parameter sets is the sufficient condition for this reduction; freezing ensures that the two sets remain equal throughout training. Modality-specific updates that make the slots differ prevent exact sharing of the affected parameters. Unfreezing parameters that remain tied preserves their equality. Under symmetric initialization, controls this weighting rather than the number of distinct learned reader states; this is the interpretation of the sweep in Figure 6. In the symmetric training formulation, each query receives the same gradient g. single tied embedding instead receives θLtied = Kg; scaling this gradient by 1/K restores the original per-query updates under matched optimizer settings. Sharing frozen Transformer slots reduces total stored parameters by 49.9%, from 606.31M to 303.95M, while retaining both visual token streams. Merging the symmetric queries further reduces trainable parameters from 4.098K to 3.074K. Both optimizations preserve the models predictions under the equivalence conditions above. 14 D. Additional parameter ablations Across the settings in Figure 6, ReMoT is least sensitive to the number of fusion queries. Varying from 1 to 4 yields eight-group averages between 90.95% and 91.21%, spread of only 0.26 percentage points. Under query symmetry, controls the attention weight of the fusion state (Appendix C). The sweep shows that readout accuracy is stable across these weighting choices. Interaction timing has larger effect. With nine initial isolated blocks, the average reaches 91.21%, up 1.11 percentage points from 90.10% with immediate interaction (s = 0). This gain suggests that an initial period of independent processing helps each view develop its own forensic cues before exchanging evidence. All tested settings with 6 12 exceed 90%, and every tested setting with 15 falls below 89%. This pattern supports an intermediate transition that leaves enough layers for cross-view exchange. The patch-radius sweep is less sensitive. Accuracy exceeds 90% for {3, 5, 7}, with modest drop at the widest tested radius and lower score of 89.78% at = 1. These results support using local neighborhood with enough spatial context for cross-view patch exchange. E. Robustness evaluation details We evaluate ReMoT and 11 baseline detectors (NPR, UnivFD, FatFormer, SAFE, C2P-CLIP, AIDE, DRCT, AlignedForensics, Effort, DDA, and OmniAID) on the original GenImage validation set, Mirage-Test, and Chameleon. JPEG re-encoding at quality factors {90, 80, 70, 60} and Gaussian blur with radii {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} are applied independently to decoded RGB images, before each detectors resizing, cropping, and normalization. Both real and generated images undergo the same processing, using Pillows default JPEG encoder and GaussianBlur filter. Blur radii are measured in source-image pixels, so their relative strength depends on image resolution. Together with the unmodified baseline, this gives nine conditions per method and benchmark. We retain the fixed threshold of 0.5 and the subset averaging protocol of Appendix A. None in the JPEG plots denotes the baseline condition, not reencoding at quality 100.
